Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

issues.item: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other selected items describe fear-based reactivity, hypervigilance, sexual trauma triggers, and intrusive/reliving memory phenomena after rape. In that context, prominent risk-taking pulls in the opposite direction of the otherwise avoidance/vigilance-focused presentation and is not supported by appraisals or maladaptive-strategy items. This creates a within-node and cross-node coherence problem.

vignette: As she navigated the dusty fields of her family's farm, 61-year-old Rohini couldn't help but feel a sense of unease wash over her. It had been years since the night that changed everything - the night she was raped by a stranger who broke into their farmhouse while her husband was away working late shifts. But despite the passing time, the memories still lingered, and the smallest trigger could send her spiraling back to that moment. For Rohini, dogs were one of those triggers. She had always loved animals, but now the sound of barking or the sight of a dog's wagging tail made her skin crawl. It was as if her body reacted before her mind even had time to process what she was seeing - her heart racing, her palms growing sweaty, and her breath catching in her throat. She couldn't explain why dogs in particular brought back the memories so vividly, but she suspected it had something to do with the sound of footsteps outside her window that night, heavy and deliberate like paws on dry earth. Sometimes, without warning, the full memory would come flooding back - the feeling of being pinned down, the taste of dirt in her mouth, and the sound of her own muffled screams. It was as if something in her surroundings had unlocked a door she thought she'd closed forever, and suddenly she was reliving that night all over again. Rohini described it like a film playing on repeat, the scenes unfolding with crystal clarity no matter how hard she tried to shake them off. Rohini's memories were so real that when she recalled them, she felt as though the event was happening right now - her mind disoriented and detached from reality. Her husband, Raj, had grown concerned about her increasing withdrawal from their intimate life together. What frightened Rohini most was the thought of being vulnerable again, of losing control in a moment of physical closeness. She longed to be free from this constant hypervigilance, but every time Raj touched her unexpectedly or initiated sex, she would recoil with alarm, her body primed for danger. Sleep had become an elusive luxury, too. Rohini found herself lying awake at night, ears perked up and eyes scanning the darkness for potential threats. Her mind was a jumble of worst-case scenarios - burglars creeping through the shadows, animals breaking free from their enclosures - all fueling her need to stay alert and vigilant. As the months went by, Rohini's avoidance behaviors had begun to take a toll on her daily life. She stopped taking care of the family farm, fearing that the isolation would leave her too vulnerable to attack. Her relationships with friends and family began to fray as she became increasingly withdrawn and isolated. Even simple tasks like grocery shopping or social gatherings became overwhelming challenges. Rohini's husband had been patient and supportive, but he couldn't understand why his wife continued to struggle so deeply. Why couldn't she just move on from the past? It was only when Rohini realized that her fears were still very real - and very much present in every waking moment - that she finally felt ready to seek help. She hoped therapy could teach her how to manage these triggers, to quiet the constant threat monitoring in her mind and rediscover a sense of safety in her own body. As she sat in the therapist's office for the first time, Rohini hesitated before speaking the words out loud - "I'm still trapped that night." The weight of those memories had held her hostage for far too long; it was time to confront them head-on and start rebuilding a life free from fear.
